questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a eukaryotic cell from a prokaryotic cell?
options: A nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles
A cell membrane that encloses the cytoplasm
Ribosomes that make proteins from amino acids
DNA that carries the cell's genetic information
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus and have membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria. All cells, prokaryotic and eukaryotic, have a cell membrane, ribosomes and DNA.

questions.stem: Which organisms are prokaryotes?
options: Algae, including green seaweeds
Fungi, including yeasts and moulds
Protists, including amoebae
Bacteria, including cyanobacteria
questions.explanation: Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. Algae, fungi and protists are all eukaryotes, even when they are single-celled, because their cells have a nucleus.

questions.stem: Why are prokaryotes significant as the first life on Earth in the Archaean Eon?
options: They appeared only after eukaryotes had already produced oxygen in the oceans
They left the first hard shells and bones, which formed the oldest index fossils
They were the only life for well over a billion years and began changing the atmosphere
They were large, complex organisms that quickly colonised the land in the Archaean Eon
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes were Earth's only life for a very long time, and photosynthetic cyanobacteria, which built stromatolites, released the oxygen that transformed the atmosphere and oceans. This made later complex life possible. They had no shells or bones.

questions.stem: In the fossil record, how does the appearance of eukaryotes compare with that of prokaryotes?
options: Eukaryotes appear before prokaryotes, which evolved from simpler eukaryotes
Eukaryotes appear more than a billion years after the earliest prokaryotes
Eukaryotes appear at the same time as the earliest prokaryotes in the rocks
Eukaryotes appear a few thousand years after the earliest prokaryotes
questions.explanation: Evidence of prokaryotic life goes back about 3.5 to 3.7 billion years, but convincing fossils of eukaryotes are much younger, by more than a billion years. Prokaryotes evolved first, and eukaryotes arose from them.

questions.stem: According to endosymbiotic theory, how did mitochondria originate?
options: A larger cell engulfed an aerobic bacterium, which lived on inside it
A cell's nucleus divided in two, and one part became a mitochondrion
A virus infected a cell and built mitochondria from the cell's proteins
A cell's membrane folded inwards and pinched off to form mitochondria
questions.explanation: The theory proposes that an ancestral cell took in a bacterium that used oxygen in respiration, and instead of being digested it lived inside the host. Over time it became the mitochondrion. Chloroplasts are thought to have arisen the same way from cyanobacteria.

questions.stem: Which observation is evidence that chloroplasts were once free-living cyanobacteria?
options: They contain chlorophyll, which is found in every eukaryotic cell type
They are found in animal cells, as well as in plant and algal cells
They are made new by the nucleus whenever the cell needs more of them
They have their own circular DNA and divide by splitting, like bacteria
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts carry their own small circular chromosome, have bacterial-type ribosomes and double membranes, and reproduce by dividing in two, as bacteria do. A cell cannot build a chloroplast from scratch. Animal cells lack chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Nearly all eukaryotes have mitochondria, or traces of them, but only algae and plants have chloroplasts. What does this suggest about the order of events?
options: Mitochondria were acquired first, and chloroplasts later in one lineage
Chloroplasts were acquired first, and mitochondria later in one lineage
Both were acquired at once, and animals later lost their mitochondria
Neither came from bacteria, since they occur in different organisms
questions.explanation: If mitochondria are almost universal in eukaryotes, the common ancestor must already have had them. Chloroplasts occur only in a sub-group, so they were taken up later by a cell that already had mitochondria. Animals did not lose mitochondria.

questions.stem: An antibiotic that blocks bacterial ribosomes also slows protein-making inside human mitochondria, but not in the rest of the cytoplasm. How does this support endosymbiotic theory?
options: Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes, as expected if they came from bacteria
Mitochondrial ribosomes resemble cytoplasmic ribosomes, as expected if they formed in the cell
The antibiotic kills the mitochondria, so they must be bacteria living in the cell today
The antibiotic enters the nucleus, so mitochondria must be made under nuclear control
questions.explanation: Mitochondria make some of their own proteins on ribosomes that are bacterial in type, unlike the ribosomes in the cytoplasm. This shared sensitivity fits a bacterial ancestry. Mitochondria are not separate living bacteria today; they cannot survive outside the cell.

questions.stem: Which scientist is best known for developing and promoting endosymbiotic theory from the late 1960s?
options: Alfred Wegener
Marie Tharp
Lynn Margulis
Stanley Miller
questions.explanation: Lynn Margulis gathered evidence from cell biology and microbiology for the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts by endosymbiosis, and the idea became widely accepted after DNA studies supported it. Stanley Miller is known for experiments on the origin of organic molecules.

questions.stem: How did the rise of oxygen in the atmosphere and oceans help eukaryotes become larger and more complex?
options: It blocked all ultraviolet radiation at once, so cells no longer needed nuclei
It cooled the oceans, so larger cells could hold more dissolved nutrients
It allowed aerobic respiration, which releases far more energy from food
It allowed photosynthesis to begin, which had been impossible before oxygen
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria releases many times more usable energy from each glucose molecule than anaerobic pathways, which can support bigger cells and, later, multicellular bodies. Photosynthesis came before free oxygen, since it produced the oxygen.

questions.stem: The Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago, marked the first lasting build-up of free oxygen in the atmosphere. What caused it?
options: Oxygen released by volcanoes increased sharply as the mantle became much hotter
Oxygen was split from carbon dioxide by lightning in the early, stormy atmosphere
Oxygen was released by eukaryotic animals breathing out in the shallow seas
Oxygen released by photosynthesising cyanobacteria exceeded what was being used up
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria had been releasing oxygen for a long time, but it was used up reacting with dissolved iron and volcanic gases. Once these sinks were overwhelmed, oxygen began to accumulate. Animals use oxygen rather than release it.

questions.stem: Before about 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen-producing cyanobacteria already existed, yet free oxygen did not build up in the air. Which evidence helps explain the delay?
options: Thick banded iron formations show oxygen reacting with dissolved iron in seawater
Thick coal seams show oxygen being locked up in plants growing on the land
Thick limestone reefs show oxygen being stored inside the skeletons of corals
Thick salt deposits show oxygen being removed as seawater evaporated quickly
questions.explanation: Oxygen released into the oceans reacted with dissolved iron to form insoluble iron oxides, which settled as banded iron formations. Only when this iron and other sinks were used up could oxygen build up in the atmosphere. Land plants and corals came much later.

questions.stem: What advantage did sexual reproduction give early eukaryotes?
options: It produced more genetic variation, so populations could adapt faster
It produced identical offspring, so useful features were never lost
It removed the need for mitochondria, so cells used less energy
It allowed cells to photosynthesise, so they could live in the dark
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction combines genes from two parents, producing varied offspring on which natural selection can act. This is thought to have helped eukaryotes diversify. Identical offspring come from asexual reproduction.

questions.stem: The Ediacara Hills in the Flinders Ranges preserve some of the oldest known large, complex multicellular organisms. What does their age tell us about the history of life?
options: Large multicellular life appeared first, before any single-celled organisms
Large multicellular life appeared at the same time as the first prokaryotes
Large multicellular life appeared only after the dinosaurs became extinct
Large multicellular life appeared only late, long after the first eukaryotes
questions.explanation: The Ediacaran organisms lived shortly before the Cambrian, roughly 3 billion years after the first prokaryotes and long after the first eukaryotes. Life stayed microscopic for most of Earth's history, and large bodies came only near the end of the Precambrian.

questions.stem: Microfossils of single cells about 100 micrometres across with ornamented walls occur in rocks about 1.5 billion years old. Why do scientists cautiously interpret them as eukaryotes?
options: They contain preserved mitochondria and nuclei, which prove they are eukaryotic cells
They are smaller than all known prokaryotes, so they must belong to a different group
They contain chlorophyll, which only eukaryotes have, so their identity is certain
They are larger and more complex than most prokaryotes, though nuclei are not preserved
questions.explanation: Large size and complex, ornamented walls are typical of eukaryotic cells, but internal structures such as nuclei are rarely preserved, so the identification relies on indirect evidence. This is why the timing of eukaryote origins is still debated. Cyanobacteria also contain chlorophyll.

questions.stem: What are ecosystem services?
options: Payments that farmers make to the government for using water from rivers
Laboratory techniques used to measure the health of polluted ecosystems
Processes in ecosystems that transform resources in ways that benefit humans
Government agencies that manage national parks and protect native species
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are the benefits people gain from natural processes, such as pollination, purifying water, forming soil and regulating climate. They are provided by ecosystems themselves, not by agencies or payments.

questions.stem: Flowering almond orchards depend on honey bees and other insects to set a crop. Which ecosystem service does this illustrate?
options: Decomposition
Soil formation
Flood control
Pollination
questions.explanation: Bees carry pollen between flowers, allowing fertilisation and nut production. Without pollinators, the yield of almonds and many fruit and vegetable crops would fall sharply. Decomposition and soil formation are different services.

questions.stem: Mangrove forests line sheltered tropical and subtropical coasts. Which pair of ecosystem services do they provide?
options: Supply fresh drinking water and remove salt from the open ocean
Shelter coasts from storm waves and act as nurseries for young fish
Raise the salinity of coastal water and prevent fish from breeding
Increase coastal erosion and release stored carbon into the air
questions.explanation: Mangrove roots slow waves and trap sediment, reducing erosion and storm damage, and their tangled roots shelter juvenile fish and crustaceans, many of which support fisheries. Mangrove soils also store large amounts of carbon.

questions.stem: Insect-eating bats and birds living in remnant bush near farms eat many crop pests each night. Which statement best describes the benefit?
options: They provide natural pest control, reducing crop losses and insecticide use
They provide pollination, so crops need fewer flowers to produce fruit
They provide soil formation, breaking down rock into fine mineral grains
They provide water purification, filtering farm run-off before it reaches creeks
questions.explanation: Predators that feed on crop pests keep pest numbers lower, so farmers lose less to pests and can spray less, saving money and protecting other species. This is pest control, a regulating service.

questions.stem: Seagrass meadows and tidal marshes store carbon in their sediments, sometimes for thousands of years. Which ecosystem service is this?
options: Food provision by producing grain crops in coastal wetlands
Cultural value by providing scenery for coastal tourism
Flood creation by trapping water behind sediment banks
Climate regulation by storing carbon away from the atmosphere
questions.explanation: By taking up carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and burying organic matter in waterlogged sediment, these 'blue carbon' ecosystems help regulate climate. Clearing or degrading them can release the stored carbon.

questions.stem: Bacteria living in the root nodules of legumes such as clover convert nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use. How does this benefit farmers?
options: It removes carbon from the soil, making the soil less acidic
It adds nitrogen to the soil, reducing the need for fertiliser
It removes nitrogen from the soil, preventing waterlogging
It adds phosphorus to the soil, replacing all other nutrients
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation by these bacteria makes nitrogen available to the plants and, when residues break down, to later crops. This is why legumes are used in crop rotations. It does not supply phosphorus.

questions.stem: Cattle dung in Australian pastures once lay on the surface for months, breeding flies and smothering grass. Dung beetles were introduced from overseas to bury it. Which services do the beetles provide?
options: Pollination of pasture grasses and faster growth of cattle herds
Removal of carbon dioxide from the air and cooler local climate
Purification of river water and protection of coasts from storms
Nutrient cycling into the soil and reduced breeding sites for flies
questions.explanation: By burying dung, beetles return nitrogen and other nutrients to the soil, aerate it and remove the moist dung pats in which bush flies breed. Australia's native dung beetles were adapted to marsupial dung, so they did little to break down cattle dung.

questions.stem: Forested water catchments supply many cities with drinking water that needs relatively little treatment. Why does keeping the catchment forested matter?
options: Forest cover stops all rain soaking into the soil, so more water flows straight into the reservoir
Forest animals drink the polluted water, so only clean water is left to flow into the reservoir
Forest soils filter water and limit erosion, so less sediment and fewer pollutants reach the reservoir
Forest trees add chlorine to the water, so it is disinfected before it reaches the reservoir
questions.explanation: Vegetation and deep forest soils slow run-off, trap sediment and allow microbes to break down contaminants, so water reaches reservoirs cleaner. Clearing the catchment would mean costly extra treatment. Forests increase infiltration, not stop it.

questions.stem: A city found that protecting and restoring the forests of its water catchment would cost far less than building a large filtration plant. What does this example show about ecosystem services?
options: They have no economic value, because nature provides them free to everyone in the region
They can always be fully replaced by technology at a lower cost than keeping the ecosystem
They are only worth protecting where no people live, because cities destroy them anyway
They have real economic value that can be compared with the cost of engineered replacements
questions.explanation: Comparing the cost of protecting a natural service with the cost of replacing it shows that ecosystems have measurable economic value. Because they are often free to use, they tend to be undervalued until they are lost.

questions.stem: Mangroves along a tropical coast are cleared to build shrimp ponds. Some years later a storm surge causes heavy flooding, and local fish catches have fallen. Which analysis is best?
options: Short-term income from the ponds came at the cost of storm protection and fish nurseries
The ponds improved storm protection, so the flooding must have had an unrelated cause
The fall in fish catches was caused by the storm surge, so the ponds played no part
The ponds increased fish nurseries, so catches fell only because of overfishing at sea
questions.explanation: Clearing mangroves removed the vegetation that absorbed wave energy and sheltered young fish, so the coast became more exposed and fisheries declined. The ponds produced income, but the lost services carried costs borne by the wider community.

questions.stem: A district relies on wild native bees as well as honey bees to pollinate its crops. A disease then sharply reduces honey bee numbers. Why might crop yields fall less than expected?
options: Diseases of honey bees make the crop flowers produce more of their own pollen
Many pollinator species do similar jobs, so others can partly take over
Crops no longer need pollination once honey bee numbers fall sharply
Native bees can pollinate only native plants, so they cannot help crops
questions.explanation: When several species provide the same service, the loss of one can be partly offset by the others. This is why biodiversity acts as insurance for ecosystem services. A crop that depends on a single pollinator is far more vulnerable.

questions.stem: A farmer keeps strips of native vegetation along fence lines and creeks rather than clearing every paddock. Which outcome is the farmer most likely to gain?
options: More weeds in the crop, because native plants always spread into paddocks
Lower soil carbon, because native plants remove carbon from nearby soils
Habitat for pest predators and pollinators, and less run-off reaching the creek
A higher water table under every paddock, which brings salt to the surface
questions.explanation: Native vegetation shelters insect-eating birds, predatory insects and native bees, and plants beside creeks trap sediment and nutrients in run-off. Deep-rooted native plants help keep water tables down, reducing rather than causing salinity.

questions.stem: Wetlands along a river slow floodwaters and trap sediment. If they are drained for farmland, which change downstream is most likely?
options: Lower, slower flood peaks and clearer water
No change, since rivers control their own flow
More fish, since the water flows more quickly
Higher, faster flood peaks and muddier water
questions.explanation: Wetlands store floodwater and release it slowly, and their plants trap sediment and nutrients. Draining them removes this storage and filtering, so floods downstream rise faster and water quality falls.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cultural ecosystem service?
options: Floodwater stored in a river's riverside wetlands
Spiritual and recreational value of a coastal landscape
Timber harvested from a plantation forest each year
Nitrogen fixed by bacteria in the roots of legumes
questions.explanation: Cultural services are the non-material benefits people gain from nature, such as recreation, inspiration, spiritual value and scenery. Timber is a provisioning service, and nitrogen fixation and flood storage are supporting and regulating services.

questions.stem: Why do the benefits of ecosystem services often depend on high biodiversity?
options: Only rare species provide services, so common species add nothing to the ecosystem
High biodiversity stops all natural processes, so the ecosystem stays exactly the same
High biodiversity means fewer decomposers, so nutrients stay locked in dead material
Many species carry out the processes, and diverse systems recover better from disturbance
questions.explanation: Pollination, decomposition, pest control and nutrient cycling are carried out by many interacting species. Diverse systems tend to be more productive and more resilient, recovering faster after drought, fire or disease.

questions.stem: An agricultural scientist shows that a nearby area of native woodland supports wasps that parasitise caterpillar pests in a neighbouring crop. How might this understanding influence decisions on the farm?
options: The farmer may spray the woodland, as the wasps will eat the crop instead
The farmer may plant more caterpillar food plants, to increase pest numbers
The farmer may keep the woodland and spray less, relying partly on the wasps
The farmer may clear the woodland, as the wasps will move into the crop anyway
questions.explanation: Knowing that the woodland supplies a pest-control service gives the farmer an economic reason to keep it and to use fewer broad-spectrum insecticides, which would also kill the beneficial wasps. Clearing the woodland would remove the wasps' habitat.

questions.stem: Which list contains only regulating ecosystem services?
options: Recreation, scenery and spiritual value
Food crops, medicines and firewood
Pollination, water purification and pest control
Timber, fresh water and fish from a river
questions.explanation: Regulating services are the benefits from natural processes being kept in check, such as pollination, purifying water, controlling pests and regulating climate. Timber, fish, food and medicines are provisioning services, and recreation and scenery are cultural services.

questions.stem: In the Amazon basin, the rainforest takes up carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and releases water vapour that falls again as rain further inland. Which benefits does this provide?
options: Climate regulation and recycling of rainfall across the region
Increased flooding and higher carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Lower rainfall and cooler oceans along the South American coast
Greater soil erosion and faster run-off into the Amazon River
questions.explanation: The forest stores carbon, acting as a carbon sink, and transpiration returns much of the rainfall to the air, where it is carried inland and falls again. Large-scale clearing can reduce both services, releasing carbon and lowering regional rainfall.

questions.stem: Living stromatolites grow today at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, Western Australia. Which organisms build them?
options: Molluscs, which build their shells layer on layer
Tube worms, which cement sand grains into tubes
Cyanobacteria, in mats that trap and bind sediment
Corals, which secrete calcium carbonate skeletons
questions.explanation: Stromatolites are layered mounds built as mats of cyanobacteria trap sediment and grow upwards through it, layer by layer. Fossil stromatolites are among the oldest evidence of life, and the cyanobacteria that built them produced oxygen by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which feature suited prokaryotes to being the first life in the oceans of the Archaean Eon?
options: Complex bodies with tissues for gathering nutrients
Small, simple cells able to live without free oxygen
Large cells with mitochondria that needed much oxygen
Hard outer skeletons that blocked ultraviolet light
questions.explanation: The Archaean atmosphere and oceans had almost no free oxygen, and early prokaryotes obtained energy by anaerobic processes. Mitochondria, which use oxygen, appeared only later in eukaryotes, and hard skeletons came much later again.

questions.stem: Comparisons of DNA and proteins suggest that the host cell which took in the ancestor of mitochondria was most closely related to which group?
options: Fungi
Archaea
Cyanobacteria
Viruses
questions.explanation: Genetic evidence places the host cell among, or close to, the archaea, while mitochondria descend from bacteria. A eukaryotic cell therefore combines two prokaryotic lineages. Fungi are themselves eukaryotes, so they cannot be the ancestor.

questions.stem: In a eucalypt forest, fungi and bacteria break down fallen leaves, branches and dead animals. Which benefit to people does this ecosystem service provide?
options: Nutrients are recycled, which keeps soils fertile for plants
Nutrients are destroyed, which stops weeds invading the forest
Carbon is turned into oxygen, which refills the atmosphere
Water is made salty, which protects the forest from insects
questions.explanation: Decomposers break dead material down and release nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients back into the soil, where plants take them up again. Without decomposition, nutrients would stay locked in litter and soils would lose fertility. Nutrients are recycled, not destroyed.
